title: Ensure the cluster-admin ClusterRole is only used when required
description: The RBAC cluster-admin ClusterRole grants full administrative authority across cluster resources and should be assigned only to approved users, groups, or service accounts with a documented operational need. For GKE Autopilot clusters, the control should focus on limiting RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments to cluster-admin, not on removing or modifying the built in ClusterRole itself. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.1 Ensure the cluster-admin ClusterRole is only used when required

audit.command: Review all Kubernetes RBAC bindings that assign the cluster-admin ClusterRole. This review should include ClusterRoleBinding objects, which grant access across the cluster, and namespaced RoleBinding objects, which can bind the cluster-admin ClusterRole within a specific namespace. List all ClusterRoleBinding subjects bound to cluster-admin: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json \ | jq -r ' ["BINDING", "SUBJECT_KIND", "SUBJECT_NAME", "SUBJECT_NAMESPACE"], ( .items[] | select(.roleRef.kind=="ClusterRole" and .roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name as $binding | ...

remediation.command: For each cluster-admin binding, replace broad access with a least privilege Role or ClusterRole that grants only the required API groups, resources, and verbs. Bind the replacement role to the approved user, group, IAM service account, or Kubernetes ServiceAccount first, validate access, and then remove the unnecessary cluster-admin binding. • Identify all ClusterRoleBinding and RoleBinding objects that assign the cluster-admin ClusterRole, including both cluster wide and namespace level bindings. • Review each bound user, group, IAM service account, or Kubernetes ServiceAccount to confirm whether full administrative access is still required and documented. • Replace cluster-admin access where possible with a least privilege Role or ClusterRole that grants only the required API groups, resources, and verbs.

title: Avoid granting cluster admin level access through the system:masters group
description: The special Kubernetes group system:masters should not be used to grant cluster-admin level access to users, groups, or service accounts. In GKE Autopilot, administrative access should be granted through explicit RBAC bindings and limited to the minimum permissions required. The system:masters group is a default Kubernetes group, and adding custom subjects to it gives those subjects access to do anything to any resource in the cluster. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. The default cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding is expected and ignored.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.6 Avoid granting cluster admin level access through the system:masters group

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .name "system:masters"}}{{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | grep -v '^$' | grep -Evx 'cluster-admin' | sort -u)
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Remediate custom system:masters usage by replacing it with explicit, auditable RBAC assignments. Do not remove the default cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding to system:masters, because it supports Kubernetes system functionality. Instead, remove custom paths that add users, groups, service accounts, or client certificates to system:masters, and grant required access through least privilege Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, or ClusterRoleBindings. • Remove any custom RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding that references system:masters, after confirming it is not a required system binding. • Remove system:masters from identity provider mappings, certificate subject groups, or other external authentication sources used for cluster access. • Replace required administrative access with explicit RBAC bindings to cluster-admin only where full cluster access is justified.

title: Avoid binding RBAC roles to unauthenticated users and groups
description: Avoid non-default RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding objects that grant permissions to the system:anonymous user or the related system:unauthenticated group. These subjects represent unauthenticated Kubernetes API requests and should not receive additional RBAC access to cluster resources. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. The built-in system:public-info-viewer binding is ignored.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.8 Avoid binding RBAC roles to unauthenticated users and groups

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .name "system:anonymous"}}{{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{if eq .name "system:unauthenticated"}}{{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | grep -v '^$' | grep -Evx 'system:public-info-viewer' | sort -u)
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Remediate any non-default RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding returned by the audit by removing unauthenticated access and replacing it with authenticated, least privilege RBAC access. Bindings to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated should not be used for normal cluster operations because they can grant Kubernetes API permissions to unauthenticated requests. • Review each returned binding and identify the referenced Role or ClusterRole, including the API groups, resources, and verbs granted. • Delete unnecessary non-default bindings to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated after confirming they are not required for cluster operation.

title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
description: Kubernetes Secrets can contain sensitive application credentials, configuration values, certificates, and legacy service account tokens. Access to these Secrets should be restricted to the smallest practical set of users, groups, service accounts, and workloads to reduce the risk of credential exposure, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to cluster or external resources. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.2 Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required

audit.command: Review RBAC permissions that grant read access to Secrets in GKE Autopilot clusters. The audit should identify where get, list, or watch permissions on the core API secrets resource are defined, how those permissions are assigned through bindings, and which users, groups, or service accounts receive the access. The review should also account for broad default roles, wildcard rules, default groups, and shared or default service accounts, because these can unintentionally expose Secrets beyond the intended operational need.

remediation.command: Remediate Secret access by replacing broad or unnecessary RBAC permissions with narrowly defined access that supports only the required workload, user, or operational function. The remediation process should focus on reducing get, list, and watch permissions on the core API secrets resource, especially where access is inherited through broad roles, wildcard rules, shared service accounts, or default service accounts. Changes should be validated before removal to avoid disrupting applications, controllers, operators, or required platform services. • Remove unnecessary Secret access by updating or replacing RBAC roles that grant get, list, orwatch on secrets, especially where the access is inherited through wildcard resources or wildcard verbs. • Replace broad Secret permissions with least privilege Roles or ClusterRoles that grant only the required API group, resource, and verb.

title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used
description: The Kubernetes default service account should not be actively used by application workloads. Instead, each workload should use a dedicated Kubernetes service account so permissions can be explicitly assigned, audited, and reviewed. Create a dedicated Kubernetes service account for each workload that requires Kubernetes API access, and avoid relying on the namespace default service account. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Fails when a default service account does not set automountServiceAccountToken: false or is bound to a Role/ClusterRole.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.4 Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used

audit.command:
sa=$(kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{if eq .metadata.name "default"}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.automountServiceAccountToken}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
rb=$(kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{$bn:=.metadata.namespace}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .kind "ServiceAccount"}}{{if eq .name "default"}}{{if .namespace}}{{.namespace}}{{else}}{{$bn}}{{end}} {{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$sa" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gmp-system|gmp-public|gke-[a-z0-9-]+)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && $2!="false" {print "automount: " $1}')
bad2=$(printf '%s
' "$rb" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gmp-system|gmp-public|gke-[a-z0-9-]+)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex {print "binding: " $0}')
if [ -z "$bad$bad2" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
%s
' "$bad" "$bad2" | grep . | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Each workload that requires Kubernetes API access should have its own service account with narrowly defined permissions. Workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access should disable automatic token mounting to reduce unnecessary credential exposure. For Google Cloud API access, use Workload Identity Federation for GKE instead of relying on static credentials in Pods. • Create dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for workloads that require Kubernetes API access • Update workload manifests to specify serviceAccountName instead of relying on the namespace default service account • Remove RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments from the default service account that are not needed • Set automountServiceAccountToken=false for Pods that do not need to communicate with the Kubernetes API server • Configure the namespace default service account with automountServiceAccountToken: false ...

title: Ensure service account tokens are mounted only when Pods require Kubernetes API access
description: Kubernetes service account tokens should be mounted in Pods only when the workload explicitly requires authenticated access to the Kubernetes API server. For workloads that do not need API server access, disable token mounting to reduce unnecessary credential exposure inside the Pod. automountServiceAccountToken controls whether Kubernetes injects a service account credential token into the Pod, and its default value is true. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.5 Ensure service account tokens are mounted only when Pods require Kubernetes API access

audit.command: Review Kubernetes service accounts and Pods in each namespace in the GKE Autopilot cluster to confirm that service account tokens are mounted only where the workload requires authenticated access to the Kubernetes API server. The audit should verify both the service account configuration and the Pod specification, because token mounting can be controlled at either level. The automountServiceAccountToken field defaults to true, so workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access should explicitly set it to false.

remediation.command: Remediate by disabling service account token mounting and assigning API access only to workloads that require it. Pods that do not need to communicate with the Kubernetes API server should set automountServiceAccountToken=false, and workloads that do need API access should use a dedicated Kubernetes service account with narrowly assigned RBAC permissions. In addition, avoiding the default service account and using separate Kubernetes service accounts per workload is recommended. • Set automountServiceAccountToken=false in Pod or workload specifications that do not require Kubernetes API access. • Create dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for workloads that require API access instead of relying on the namespace default service account. • Grant only the required RBAC permissions to those service accounts through least privilege Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, or ClusterRoleBindings.

title: Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster
description: Roles and ClusterRoles with bind, escalate, or impersonate permissions should be granted only to tightly controlled administrative or platform identities with a documented need. These permissions can allow a subject to expand effective access beyond normal RBAC assignments and should not be included in general user, workload, or automation roles. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.7 Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster

audit.command: Review Role and ClusterRole objects that grant bind, escalate, or impersonate, then trace those roles through RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects to identify the users, groups, and service accounts that receive the permissions. These verbs should be limited to documented administrative or platform use cases because bind and escalate can grant permissions beyond the caller’s current access, while impersonate can allow API requests as another subject. RBAC permissions are additive, so unnecessary access should be identified and removed.

remediation.command: Replace bind, escalate, and impersonate access with narrowly defined RBAC permissions that support only the approved administrative, platform, or automation function. Remove these verbs from general user, workload, and service account roles unless there is a valid requirement. Review changes before removal to avoid disrupting controllers, operators, CI/CD workflows, or access review processes. • Remove bind, escalate, and impersonate from Roles and ClusterRoles where they are not explicitly required. • Replace broad access with least privilege rules that define the exact API groups, resources, verbs, and namespace scope required. • Avoid granting RBAC modification permissions such as bind, escalate, create, update, or patch on rbac.authorization.k8s.io resources to service accounts unless specifically justified.

title: Avoid binding RBAC roles to all authenticated users
description: Avoid non-default RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects that grant RBAC permissions to the system:authenticated group. This group represents all authenticated Kubernetes API requests from users signed in with a Google Account, including Gmail accounts, so it should not be used for custom access grants. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. The default system:basic-user, system:discovery and system:public-info-viewer bindings are ignored.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.9 Avoid binding RBAC roles to all authenticated users

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .name "system:authenticated"}}{{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | grep -v '^$' | grep -Evx 'system:basic-user|system:discovery|system:public-info-viewer' | sort -u)
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Remove any non-default binding tosystem:authenticate identified in the audit and replace it with explicit, least privilege access for specific authenticated subjects. Do not remove the expected default ClusterRoleBindings system:basic-user, system:discovery, or system:public-info-viewer. RBAC permissions should be granted through defined users, groups, or service accounts rather than the broad system:authenticated group. • Review each non-default RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding returned by the audit and identify the referenced Role or ClusterRole. • Determine the specific API groups, resources, verbs, and namespace scope required for the affected users, tools, or automation. • Create or update a least privilege Role or ClusterRole that grants only the required access. • Bind the replacement role to a specific user, Google Group, IAM service account, or Kubernetes service account.

title: Enable application-layer Secrets encryption with Cloud KMS keys
description: Enable application layer Secrets encryption for GKE Autopilot clusters using a Cloud KMS key. This control adds customer managed encryption for Kubernetes Secret resources stored in the cluster state database, providing an additional protection layer beyond Google managed encryption at rest. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.3.1 Enable application-layer Secrets encryption with Cloud KMS keys

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(databaseEncryption.state,databaseEncryption.currentState,databaseEncryption.keyName)') || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s' "$out" | tr '\t' ' ')
if [ "${1:-}" = ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED ] && [ "${2:-}" = CURRENT_STATE_ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED ] && [ -n "${3:-}" ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: $out"; fi

remediation.command: Enable application layer encryption on the GKE Autopilot cluster when the audit shows that databaseEncryption.state is not ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED or ENCRYPTED, databaseEncryption.currentState is not CURRENT_STATE_ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED or CURRENT_STATE_ENCRYPTED, or databaseEncryption.keyName does not reference the approved Cloud KMS CryptoKey. Before enabling encryption, grant the Kubernetes Engine Service Agent permission to use the Cloud KMS key. The service agent needs the Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role so GKE can encrypt and decrypt Kubernetes Secret data in the cluster state database.

title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
description: Kubernetes Roles and ClusterRoles define what actions users, groups, and Kubernetes service accounts can perform against Kubernetes API resources in GKE Autopilot clusters. Wildcard permissions should be minimized because the * character applies broadly across API groups, resources, or verbs and can grant more access than intended. Roles should explicitly define only the API groups, resources, and verbs required for the subject’s function. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.3 Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles

audit.command: Review Kubernetes RBAC roles in GKE Autopilot clusters to identify wildcard permissions in Roles and ClusterRoles. The audit should check for * in apiGroups, resources, or verbs, because wildcard permissions can unintentionally grant access to current or future Kubernetes APIs, resources, custom resources, or actions. After identifying wildcard rules, review the related RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects to determine which users, groups, or Kubernetes service accounts receive the permissions. RBAC access should be reviewed regularly and aligned to least privilege.

remediation.command: Replace wildcard permissions with explicit RBAC rules that define only the required API groups, resources, and verbs. Remediation should focus on preserving required access while removing broad * grants that could expand privileges as APIs, resources, or CRDs are added. Validate affected users, workloads, controllers, and automation before removing wildcard access. For GKE Autopilot clusters, remediation remains focused on Kubernetes RBAC objects, including Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoleBindings. • Replace verbs: ["*"] with only the required actions, such as get, list, watch, create, update, patch, or delete. • Replace resources: ["*"] with only the required Kubernetes resources or custom resources. • Replace apiGroups: ["*"] with the specific API groups required by the subject’s function.

title: Use NetworkPolicy with built in GKE Dataplane V2 enforcement
description: NetworkPolicy enforcement is built in for GKE Autopilot clusters through GKE Dataplane V2. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects can restrict Pod to Pod, Pod to Service, ingress, and egress traffic without enabling Calico or a separate NetworkPolicy add-on. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.3.1 Use NetworkPolicy with built in GKE Dataplane V2 enforcement

audit.command: Review the GKE Autopilot cluster configuration and verify that the cluster uses GKE Dataplane V2 for built in NetworkPolicy enforcement. NetworkPolicy requires a network plugin to implement enforcement. In Autopilot clusters, GKE Dataplane V2 is enabled by default and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is always on.

remediation.command: For GKE Autopilot clusters, no remediation is required to enable NetworkPolicy enforcement because GKE Dataplane V2 is enabled by default and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement is built in. Remediation should focus on creating and maintaining NetworkPolicy resources that define the intended ingress and egress traffic rules for workloads. • Apply NetworkPolicy resources in the required namespaces to define explicit allowed traffic paths for approved workload communication. • Use default deny policies where appropriate, followed by explicit allow policies for required ingress and egress traffic. • Validate application connectivity after applying NetworkPolicy resources.

title: Use Secret Manager for external workload secret storage
description: Use Secret Manager as the preferred external storage and management service for workload secrets used by GKE Autopilot clusters. Workloads should access secrets through Secret Manager API calls using Workload Identity Federation for GKE, or through mounted volumes using the Secret Manager add-on when file based access is required. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.4.1 Use Secret Manager for external workload secret storage

audit.command: Review the GKE Autopilot secrets implementation and verify that sensitive workload secrets are stored in Secret Manager where external secret storage is required, rather than relying only on native Kubernetes Secrets. Confirm whether workloads access Secret Manager through direct API calls with Workload Identity Federation for GKE, or through mounted files using the Secret Manager add-on and SecretProviderClass resources.

remediation.command: Move externally managed workload secrets to Secret Manager and update GKE workloads to access them through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. Prefer direct Secret Manager API access through Google Cloud client libraries where the application supports it. For applications that require file based secret access, enable the Secret Manager add-on and mount secrets into Pods using SecretProviderClass and CSI volumes. • Configure applications to use Workload Identity Federation for GKE for Secret Manager access. • Use dedicated Kubernetes ServiceAccounts for workloads that need Secret Manager access. • Grant least privilege Secret Manager IAM permissions only to the required workload identities. • Enable the Secret Manager add-on when workloads need secrets mounted as files. • Migrate sensitive values out of Kubernetes Secrets where practical, then remove unused in-cluster Secret objects.

title: Use namespaces to separate workload administration and resource governance
description: Use dedicated namespaces to separate GKE Autopilot workloads by application, team, environment, or tenant. Namespaces provide a logical boundary for organizing resources and applying namespace level governance, but they should be paired with access, quota, network, and pod security controls. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.1 Use namespaces to separate workload administration and resource governance

audit.command: Run the following command and review the namespaces created in the cluster: kubectl get namespaces --show-labels Verify that user workloads are placed in dedicated namespaces based on application, environment, or tenant, rather than being deployed into the default namespace. In addition, confirm that each workload namespace has both ownership and appropriate namespace level controls, such as RBAC RoleBindings, ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, and Pod Security labels where required.

remediation.command: Create dedicated namespaces for GKE Autopilot workloads based on application, environment, or tenant boundaries. Move production workloads out of the default namespace and apply consistent namespace level governance so administration, access, and resource controls are easier to manage. • Create a dedicated namespace before deploying new application resources. • Move production workloads out of the default namespace where applicable. • Apply namespace labels for owner, application, environment, tenant, and cost allocation. • Configure least privilege RBAC using namespace level Roles and RoleBindings where possible. • Apply ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, and Pod Security labels based on workload risk and governance requirements.

title: Enable Artifact Analysis scanning for Artifact Registry container images
description: Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning for container images stored in Artifact Registry and used by GKE Autopilot workloads. This verifies that container images are scanned at the registry layer before deployment to identify known vulnerabilities in image packages, dependencies, and software components. Requires gcloud (serviceusage.services.list) for GKE_PROJECT or the default project. Repository-level scanning exclusions still need review.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.1 Enable Artifact Analysis scanning for Artifact Registry container images

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud services list --enabled ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --filter='config.name=containerscanning.googleapis.com' --format='value(config.name)') || exit 1
if [ "$v" = containerscanning.googleapis.com ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: Container Scanning API disabled"; fi

remediation.command: Enable Artifact Analysis automatic vulnerability scanning for container images stored in Artifact Registry and used by GKE Autopilot workloads. Enabling the Container Scanning API activates automatic scanning for images pushed to standard and remote Docker repositories in Artifact Registry, and it also enables the Container Analysis API for vulnerability metadata storage and retrieval. Enable the required project APIs: gcloud services enable artifactregistry.googleapis.com containerscanning.googleapis.com \ --project=$PROJECT_ID If scanning was disabled on a specific Artifact Registry repository, update the repository to allow vulnerability scanning: gcloud artifacts repositories update $REPOSITORY \ --project=$PROJECT_ID \ --location=$LOCATION \ --allow-vulnerability-scanning Note: Repeat the repository update command for each Docker repository that stores images deployed to GKE ...

title: Grant least privilege IAM access to Artifact Registry repositories
description: Restrict access to Artifact Registry repositories that store GKE Autopilot workload images. Grant users, groups, CI/CD identities, and GKE node service accounts only the IAM roles needed to pull, push, administer, or manage container images. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.2 Grant least privilege IAM access to Artifact Registry repositories

audit.command: Review IAM access for Artifact Registry Docker repositories that store images deployed to GKE Autopilot clusters. Verify that repository permissions are limited to approved users, groups, service accounts, CI/CD identities, and GKE node service accounts based on their required function. Artifact Registry access can be granted at the project level or repository level, but repository level IAM should be used when access needs to differ by application, team, environment, or repository.

remediation.command: Apply least privilege IAM access to Artifact Registry Docker repositories that store images deployed to GKE Autopilot clusters. Repository access should be limited to approved users, groups, service accounts, CI/CD identities, and GKE node service accounts based on their required function. Use repository level IAM where access should differ by application, team, environment, or repository, and avoid broad project level grants unless the same access is intentionally required across all repositories. • Grant GKE node service accounts read only access to the specific Artifact Registry repositories they need to pull workload images from by assigning roles/artifactregistry.reader at the repository level. • Grant CI/CD publishing identities access only to repositories where they need to publish images by assigning roles/artifactregistry.writer at the repository level.

title: Enforce Binary Authorization for trusted GKE container image deployments
description: Use Binary Authorization to enforce trusted image deployment policies for GKE Autopilot clusters. The policy should allow only approved container images to be deployed, based on defined admission rules such as approved image locations, trusted build or promotion processes, and required signed approvals where appropriate. Binary Authorization works with both Autopilot and Standard clusters. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.3 Enforce Binary Authorization for trusted GKE container image deployments

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(binaryAuthorization.evaluationMode)') || exit 1
if case "$v" in PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE|POLICY_BINDINGS_AND_PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE) true;; *) false;; esac; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: binaryAuthorization.evaluationMode=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Enable Binary Authorization enforcement on the GKE Autopilot cluster when the audit shows that the cluster is not using an enforcing evaluation mode. Use PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE to enforce the project Binary Authorization policy. If the cluster also uses continuous validation with policy bindings, use POLICY_BINDINGS_AND_PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE instead. Monitoring only modes should not be used as the remediation target for this control. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=$LOCATION \ --project=$PROJECT_ID \ --binauthz-evaluation-mode=PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE Export the current Binary Authorization policy to a local YAML file. The trusted image deployment rules are edited in this policy file, not directly in the GKE cluster configuration.

title: Use a custom least privilege node service account for GKE Autopilot
description: Use a custom least privilege IAM service account for GKE Autopilot nodes instead of the Compute Engine default service account. The node service account should have only the IAM permissions required for GKE system tasks, logging, monitoring, and approved image pulls. GKE recommends using a custom node service account because the Compute Engine default service account might have broader permissions than GKE requires. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.2.1 Use a custom least privilege node service account for GKE Autopilot

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(nodeConfig.serviceAccount)') || exit 1
if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" != default ] && ! printf '%s' "$v" | grep -q -- '-compute@developer\.gserviceaccount\.com$'; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: nodeConfig.serviceAccount=$v"; fi

remediation.command: For new GKE Autopilot clusters, create a custom IAM service account for nodes and grant only the permissions required for GKE node operation. At minimum, grant roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount on the project. gcloud iam service-accounts create $NODE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_NAME \ --project $PROJECT_ID gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $PROJECT_ID \ --member=serviceAccount:$NODE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT \ --role=roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount Create the Autopilot cluster with the custom node service account.

title: Enable VPC Flow Logs and Intranode Visibility
description: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet used by GKE Autopilot nodes and enable intranode visibility on the GKE cluster to improve visibility into Pod traffic. This combination allows network flow logging to include traffic between Pods, including traffic between Pods running on the same worker node. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.1 Enable VPC Flow Logs and Intranode Visibility

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(networkConfig.enableIntraNodeVisibility,subnetwork)') || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s' "$out" | tr '\t' ' ')
[ "${1:-}" = True ] || { echo "noncompliant: intranode visibility disabled"; exit 0; }
r=$GKE_LOCATION; case "$r" in *-*-*) r=${r%-*};; esac
fl=$(gcloud compute networks subnets describe "${2:?no subnetwork}" --region "$r" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(enableFlowLogs,logConfig.enable)') || exit 1
if printf '%s' "$fl" | grep -q True; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: VPC Flow Logs disabled on $2"; fi

remediation.command: Enable intranode visibility on the GKE Autopilot cluster when the audit shows that networkConfig.enableIntraNodeVisibility is not true. Enabling intranode visibility makes Pod to Pod traffic on the same node visible to the VPC network path so it can be captured by VPC Flow Logs and other VPC features. Plan the change during an approved maintenance window because enabling intranode visibility on an existing cluster can restart components in the control plane and worker nodes. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-intra-node-visibility After intranode visibility is enabled, review the subnet used by the GKE Autopilot cluster and confirm that VPC Flow Logs are enabled for that subnet.

title: Restrict GKE control plane access with authorized networks
description: Restrict GKE Autopilot control plane access by enabling authorized networks for IP based control plane endpoints and allowing only approved CIDR ranges. This reduces exposure of the Kubernetes API server by limiting which source IP ranges can reach the control plane over the configured IP endpoint. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.2 Restrict GKE control plane access with authorized networks

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig.enabled,masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig.gcpPublicCidrsAccessEnabled)') || exit 1
cidrs=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig.cidrBlocks[].cidrBlock)') || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s' "$out" | tr '\t' ' ')
if [ "${1:-}" = True ] && [ "${2:-False}" != True ] && [ -n "$cidrs" ] && ! printf '%s' "$cidrs" | grep -q '0\.0\.0\.0/0'; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: enabled=${1:-} gcpPublicCidrs=${2:-} cidrs=$cidrs"; fi

remediation.command: Enable control plane authorized networks when the audit shows that masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig is missing, does not show authorized networks as enabled, does not include approved cidrBlocks, or includes broad ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0. Authorized networks should include only trusted administrative, bastion, VPN, CI/CD, or automation source ranges that require access to the GKE Autopilot control plane IP endpoint, and use authorized networks when IP based control plane endpoints are enabled. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-master-authorized-networks \ --master-authorized-networks <authorized-cidrs> If broad access from Google Cloud external IP addresses is not explicitly approved, disable that access so external IP addresses from Google Cloud are not automatically allowed to reach the control plane.

title: Use DNS based access or private GKE control plane endpoints
description: Use DNS based access or private GKE control plane endpoints to reduce Kubernetes API server exposure. Prefer DNS based control plane access where possible, and if IP based access is required, disable the external IP based endpoint or restrict it to trusted networks only. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.3 Use DNS based access or private GKE control plane endpoints

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(controlPlaneEndpointsConfig.ipEndpointsConfig.enabled,controlPlaneEndpointsConfig.ipEndpointsConfig.enablePublicEndpoint,controlPlaneEndpointsConfig.dnsEndpointConfig.endpoint,controlPlaneEndpointsConfig.dnsEndpointConfig.allowExternalTraffic)') || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s' "$out" | tr '\t' '|' | awk -F '|' '{for(i=1;i<=4;i++) printf "%s ", ($i=="" ? "-" : $i)}')
if [ "$2" = False ]; then echo compliant
elif [ "$1" = False ] && [ "$3" != - ] && [ "$4" = True ]; then echo compliant
else echo "noncompliant: ipEndpoints=$1 publicEndpoint=$2 dnsEndpoint=$3 allowExternalTraffic=$4"; fi

remediation.command: Remediate existing GKE clusters by updating the control plane access configuration. Recreating the cluster is not required for this control. Choose the access model that matches the organization’s approved management path. Method 1: Use DNS based control plane access and disable IP based endpoint access where appropriate: gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-dns-access \ --no-enable-ip-access Method 2: Use IP based access with the external endpoint disabled and the private endpoint enabled: gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-ip-access \ --enable-private-endpoint If the public IP based endpoint must remain enabled, restrict it with authorized networks and use only approved CIDR ranges.

title: Ensure private GKE nodes are configured without external IP addresses
description: Configure GKE Autopilot nodes without external IP addresses so worker nodes are reachable only through internal network paths. Private nodes reduce direct exposure of the node network interface to external clients while still allowing the cluster to run workloads and communicate with the control plane through internal connectivity. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.4 Ensure private GKE nodes are configured without external IP addresses

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(privateClusterConfig.enablePrivateNodes)') || exit 1
if [ "$v" = True ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: privateClusterConfig.enablePrivateNodes=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Remediate by enabling private nodes at the cluster level for GKE Autopilot workloads. Private nodes provision GKE nodes with internal IP addresses only. For Autopilot clusters, update the cluster level private node configuration instead of updating individual node pools. The cluster update takes effect after GKE reschedules workloads onto nodes that match the configuration. Enable private nodes as the cluster level default for GKE Autopilot workloads: gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-private-nodes \ --enable-ip-alias If workload level placement is required, configure the workload to schedule on private nodes by using the cloud.google.com/private-node=true node selector. Note: After remediation, rerun the audit command and confirm that the cluster level default returns true.

title: Use Google managed SSL certificates for GKE Ingress TLS
description: Use Google managed SSL certificates for GKE Ingress TLS to encrypt client traffic between external users and the Google Cloud load balancer. Google provisions and renews these certificates for the configured domains, reducing manual certificate lifecycle management for supported GKE Ingress use cases. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.5 Use Google managed SSL certificates for GKE Ingress TLS

audit.command: Review public application exposure and identify workloads using Service objects of type LoadBalancer. Google managed SSL certificates for GKE Ingress apply to HTTPS load balancers created through Ingress, not TCP or UDP load balancers created directly from Service objects. Public HTTP or HTTPS workloads exposed through LoadBalancer services should be reviewed to determine whether GKE Ingress is the better TLS termination pattern.

remediation.command: Remediate public HTTPS workloads by using GKE Ingress with Google managed SSL certificates where this pattern is appropriate. This applies to HTTPS traffic terminated by the external Application Load Balancer through GKE Ingress and does not apply to TCP or UDP workloads exposed through Service objects of type LoadBalancer. • For public HTTP or HTTPS workloads exposed directly through Service objects of type LoadBalancer, evaluate whether they should be exposed through GKE Ingress so Google managed SSL certificates can be used. • Create a ManagedCertificate object in the same namespace as the Ingress and define the approved non wildcard domain names for the certificate. • Update the Ingress metadata to include the networking.gke.io/managed-certificates annotation with the ManagedCertificate resource name. Multiple managed certificates can be listed as comma separated values when needed.

title: Use Google Groups to centrally manage Kubernetes RBAC access for GKE clusters
description: Use Google Groups for RBAC to centrally manage Kubernetes RBAC access for GKE Autopilot clusters. Cluster administrators should assign Kubernetes RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding permissions to approved Google Groups rather than directly binding access to individual user email addresses. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.5.1 Use Google Groups to centrally manage Kubernetes RBAC access for GKE clusters

audit.command: Review the GKE Autopilot cluster and verify that Google Groups for RBAC is enabled and configured with the required security group. Google Groups for RBAC lets Kubernetes RBAC permissions be assigned to Google Groups managed in Google Workspace or Cloud Identity, rather than binding access directly to individual user email addresses.

remediation.command: Enable Google Groups for RBAC when the audit shows that authenticatorGroupsConfig.enabled is not true, or when securityGroup is missing or incorrect. The required security group must be named gke-security-groups@DOMAIN, and approved access groups should be nested under that security group before they are referenced in Kubernetes RBAC bindings. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --security-group=gke-security-groups@$DOMAIN After Google Groups for RBAC is enabled, update Kubernetes RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects to reference approved Google Groups as kind: Group subjects. Replace direct User bindings with group based bindings where practical, while preserving required ServiceAccount bindings for workloads, controllers, and automation.

title: Use CMEK protected StorageClasses for GKE Persistent Disk volumes
description: Use CMEK protected StorageClass objects for GKE Autopilot Persistent Disk volumes so newly provisioned Persistent Disks are encrypted with an approved Cloud KMS key. This applies to dynamically provisioned Persistent Disk volumes that use the Compute Engine Persistent Disk CSI driver and the disk-encryption-kms-key parameter. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.6.1 Use CMEK protected StorageClasses for GKE Persistent Disk volumes

audit.command: Review GKE Autopilot StorageClass objects and verify that Persistent Disk classes use the Compute Engine Persistent Disk CSI driver with an approved Cloud KMS key. The disk-encryption-kms-key parameter should contain the fully qualified Cloud KMS key resource path used to encrypt newly provisioned Persistent Disk volumes.

remediation.command: Remediate any StorageClass or Persistent Disk that does not use an approved Cloud KMS key. CMEK for GKE Autopilot Persistent Disk volumes is applied through a CMEK protected StorageClass for new dynamically provisioned volumes. Existing Persistent Disks cannot be converted to CMEK in place, so noncompliant volumes must be replaced or migrated. • Grant the Compute Engine service agent for the cluster project roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the approved Cloud KMS key. • Create a new CMEK protected StorageClass using the Persistent Disk CSI driver, pd.csi.storage.gke.io, and the approved disk-encryption-kms-key value. • Update new PersistentVolumeClaims to use the CMEK protected StorageClass. If this should be the default storage option, mark the CMEK protected StorageClass as the default only after validating the key, location, and access permissions.

title: Enforce image provenance using Binary Authorization for GKE
description: Use Binary Authorization for GKE to enforce image provenance and deploy time trust policies before container images are admitted to the GKE Autopilot cluster. Policies should allow only approved images, trusted registries, or images with required attestations from approved build, security, or release processes. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.5.1 Enforce image provenance using Binary Authorization for GKE

audit.command: Review the GKE Autopilot cluster and confirm that Binary Authorization enforcement is enabled and confirm it does not simply allow all images and that it requires approved images, trusted registries, or attestations from trusted attestors where appropriate. Binary Authorization works with GKE clusters, including Autopilot clusters, and evaluates the configured policy at deploy time.

remediation.command: Enable Binary Authorization enforcement for the GKE Autopilot cluster and configure the policy to block unapproved images at deploy time. Use approved image rules, trusted registries, or attestation based requirements aligned to the build, security scan, and release approval process. Validate the policy in dry run or a lower environment before enforcing broadly in production.

title: Rely on Autopilot RuntimeDefault seccomp; custom profiles are unsupported
description: GKE Autopilot automatically applies the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile to workload Pods, so custom seccomp profile configuration is not required for normal workloads. Custom Localhost seccomp profiles are not supported in Autopilot because GKE manages the nodes, and GKE Sandbox Pods use sandbox isolation as the security boundary instead of Pod specified seccomp rules. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.2 Rely on Autopilot RuntimeDefault seccomp; custom profiles are unsupported

audit.command: Review workload Pods to confirm that they do not specify unsupported custom seccomp profiles and do not use Unconfined unless there is a documented exception. Missing seccompProfile fields are not a finding in Autopilot because GKE applies the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile automatically. kubectl get pods -A -o json \ | jq -r ' ["NAMESPACE","POD","POD_SECCOMP","CONTAINER","CONTAINER_SECCOMP"], ( .items[] as $pod | ($pod.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type // "not-set") as $podSeccomp | $pod.spec.containers[] | [ $pod.metadata.namespace, $pod.metadata.name, $podSeccomp, .name, ...

remediation.command: For GKE Autopilot workloads, remove unsupported custom Localhost seccomp profile settings and rely on the automatically applied RuntimeDefault profile. Do not attempt to install or manage custom seccomp profiles on Autopilot nodes because GKE manages the node environment. If a workload specifies Unconfined, validate and document the requirement, then remove the override where possible so the workload uses the Autopilot default seccomp protection. For GKE Sandbox workloads, treat the sandbox as the security boundary because seccomp rules specified in the Pod manifest are ignored.

title: Require hardened security contexts for all workload Pods and containers
description: Require hardened security contexts for GKE Autopilot workload Pods and containers. Security contexts should define workload level and container level controls that reduce privilege, limit host exposure, and enforce safer runtime behavior. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.3 Require hardened security contexts for all workload Pods and containers

audit.command: Review workload Pods and controller templates to confirm hardened security contexts are explicitly defined at the Pod and container level. Focus the audit on workload namespaces and verify settings such as runAsNonRoot=true, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, privileged=false, dropped Linux capabilities where practical, and no explicit seccompProfile.type=Unconfined unless documented as an approved exception. Missing seccompProfile fields are not a finding in GKE Autopilot because Autopilot applies the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile to workload Pods by default.

remediation.command: Update workload manifests, Helm charts, overlays, or GitOps sources so hardened security contexts are defined before deployment. Apply settings at the Pod level when they apply to all containers, and use container level settings where a specific container requires a different configuration. • Set workloads to run as non root where compatible. • Set allowPrivilegeEscalation=false for workload containers. • Set privileged=false and remove host level access unless explicitly required. • Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, and use drop: ["ALL"] where the application supports it. • Set seccompProfile.type=RuntimeDefault where seccomp is explicitly defined, and remove unsupported custom Localhost seccomp profiles from GKE Autopilot workloads. Redeploy the workload and validate application behavior in a lower environment before broad rollout.

title: Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace
description: Avoid deploying GKE Autopilot workloads in the default namespace. Use dedicated namespaces to separate applications, environments, or tenants so namespace level controls can be applied consistently. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.4 Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace

audit.command: Run the following command to identify resources currently deployed in the default namespace: kubectl get all,configmaps,secrets,pvc,ingress,serviceaccounts,networkpolicies -n default Review any returned resources and determine whether they are application, environment, or tenant workloads that should be moved to a dedicated namespace. GKE supports identifying workloads running in the default namespace and migrating them to dedicated namespaces to improve reliability and security.

remediation.command: Create dedicated namespaces for GKE Autopilot workloads based on application, environment, or tenant boundaries, then migrate application resources out of the default namespace. Make updates so all workload resources explicitly specify the new target namespace. After migration, apply appropriate namespace level governance, including RBAC, ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, Pod Security labels, and ownership labels.

title: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for cluster security insights
description: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard to surface cluster and workload security insights, including workload configuration auditing, actionable security concerns, and security bulletin related findings. The dashboard provides a centralized view of security posture findings so teams can identify, prioritize, and remediate issues across eligible GKE clusters and workloads. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.7.1 Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for cluster security insights

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(securityPostureConfig.mode)') || exit 1
if case "$v" in BASIC|ENTERPRISE) true;; *) false;; esac; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: securityPostureConfig.mode=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for workload configuration auditing when the audit shows that securityPostureConfig.mode is not BASIC. GKE supports enabling configuration auditing on existing clusters by setting the security posture mode to standard, which maps to BASIC in the cluster configuration. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --security-posture=standard For new clusters, include --security-posture=standard during cluster creation when this setting must be explicitly enforced. Rerun the audit command and confirm that securityPostureConfig.mode returns BASIC. Initial configuration audit results can take up to 30 minutes to appear in the security posture dashboard and related logs.
